title: Huiwon, from a flash to a spark
description: On a four-song EP, singer-songwriter Huiwon moves from keys to bass and drums to guitar, all while making room for a smile beside slightly dirty wallpaper or a flower just beginning to open.

blocks.text: The wallpaper in Huiwon’s “2008” is a little dirty. It’s a lovely detail to keep beside someone’s smile. When the speaker puts the day back together, the room comes back too.

Singer-songwriter Huiwon (천희원) wrote all four songs on the 2025 EP 反骨商會 (반골상회) and arranged three of them. The credits follow Huiwon from the keys on “2008” to bass and drums on “soultrap.exe” and a shared guitar part on “light.” A little over a year later, the single “Birth…” takes up a different kind of small detail. Its release note gives the idea of starting again to an insect crawling along the ground.

“It’s been a long time since I’ve come across someone who feels this naturally musical,” says indiek’s publisher. The EP gives that feeling something to point to. Huiwon can write a song around an ordinary little detail and arrange it and play several of the parts.

blocks.alt: Official cover of Huiwon’s 反骨商會 EP
blocks.caption: 反骨商會 · Official EP artwork via Apple Music.

blocks.text: In “2008,” remembering has something to do with choosing what to keep. The lyric imagines picking out scenes and joining them together. The road and the sky keep returning, and so does the smile against that wallpaper. The sense of missing someone comes through in what the speaker remembers about where they were. There’s even a moment of reaching for the receiver, as if the voice were something they could take out again.

The next song has a camera of its own, though the view in “soultrap.exe” is much less inviting. The speaker compares their unsteady view to a low-resolution camera. A file extension is a funny little title detail for a song with such a raw wish to get out of one’s own skin. The EP can hold the affection of “2008” and this itch to get out, one song apart.

Lee Seo-hyeong (이서형) plays bass and Yeo Jin-woo (여진우) drums on “2008.” On “soultrap.exe,” Lee Tae-yul (이태율) plays guitar while Huiwon also handles the keyboards and MIDI. The arrangement credit changes on “Found and Lost.” Huiwon wrote it, and Heo Se-gwa (허세과) arranged it and played guitar and bass.

“Found and Lost” has a wish its speaker keeps returning to, a place they want to reach. They’d keep going even if it meant burning. That line has an echo in “Birth…,” where the speaker asks for the embers to spread. Fire goes from something they might have to go through to something they want to set in motion.

There’s a turn in “light” that makes its last few lines especially tender. The speaker asks for someone to hear their heartbeat, then asks for it to stop. At the end they want it heard again. They also ask to let a flower bloom. The Korean title 섬광 means a flash, something gone almost as soon as it appears. A flower needs longer. Both images belong in a song that keeps asking for something to stay.

Chris P, reviewing the EP for Korean Indie, hears “light” open with a voice and sparse electric guitar before it grows into a fuller rock arrangement. A voice with so little beside it is an apt setting for a plea to stay. The studio credits put Huiwon on bass and MIDI and alongside Jo Yu-ik (조유익) on guitar. Yeo Jin-woo is back on drums. Huiwon has also shared live versions of “2008” and “light,” the two ends of the EP.

blocks.alt: Official cover of Huiwon’s Birth… single
blocks.caption: Birth… · Official single artwork via Apple Music.

blocks.text: 태동, the Korean title, can mean movement in the womb or the first stirrings of something new. There’s nothing grand about the way the release note pictures it. An insect crawls along the ground. The song’s speaker imagines being woken even if it hurts and asks the embers to spread. That little creature feels at home beside a request to get moving, however close to the ground the first movement happens to be.

Huiwon wrote and arranged “Birth…”. Song Ju-won (송주원) plays guitar and Shin Ji-min (신지민) plays drums. Lee Seo-hyeong, the bassist on “2008,” is here too. It’s a small continuity between a song that keeps calling back a familiar place and one that wants to see how far it can go.

There’s an especially gentle request in “Birth…” about regret. The speaker asks to put it off a little longer. They want to move faster, and there’s room in that wish for how hard it might be to look back. The dots at the end of the title feel right there. The song has time for the person still getting started.

editorial.contribution: The feature gives readers two ways into the same songs. It follows Huiwon’s changing studio roles and names the players who share the work. It also follows what the speakers ask for, from recovering a voice in “2008” to having a heartbeat heard in “light” and asking for more time before regret in “Birth…”. The strongest connection is the change in what fire means across releases. In “Found and Lost,” burning is a risk the speaker accepts. In “Birth…,” spreading the embers is something the speaker asks for.
comparisons: Joshua Minsoo Kim’s “Long Season” makes individual contributions legible within a collective recording. “The private worlds of youra” opens on a specific studio encounter and closes with the artist’s account of a flute part. The Huiwon feature’s opening and ending come from the lyrics, with the publisher’s personal response and the collaborators’ credits establishing a different kind of intimacy.
